extracted.intended_audience: philosophers of science and mathematics; graduate students and researchers in philosophy of mathematics
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and formalizes Kitcher’s account of scientific explanation as unification (argument/derivation patterns, systematizations E(K), and criteria for ranking systematizations), and discusses its fit to mathematical practice (examples from real algebraic geometry).

rubrics_metrics.name: Theory of explanation should account for understanding and dispute resolution
rubrics_metrics.description: A theory of explanation should (1) account for how science advances our understanding of the world and (2) help us in evaluating or arbitrating disputes in science. (Kitcher, 1981)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kitcher points to these two desiderata as minimal tests for any account of explanation; critiques of other models (e.g. covering law) are measured against them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanation as unification (basic intuition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Science increases understanding by reducing the number of independent phenomena we must accept as brute — more comprehensible worlds have fewer independent phenomena (Friedman 1974); Kitcher modifies this to emphasize reduction in the number of argument/derivation patterns used while maximizing phenomena explained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kitcher: E(K) is a set of derivations that makes the best tradeoff between minimizing the number of patterns of derivation employed and maximizing the number of conclusions generated (Kitcher, 1989, p.432).

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanations are derivations, not isolated argument pairs
rubrics_metrics.description: On the systematization account, explanations are derivations — sequences of statements whose status (premise or derived) and rules are specified — rather than mere premise–conclusion pairs (Hempelian view).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An ideal explanation shows how premises yield the conclusion; this makes explanatoriness a global property (belonging to the best systematization) rather than a purely local property of an argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptability of a set of derivations relative to K
rubrics_metrics.description: A set of derivations is acceptable relative to K just in case every step in the derivations is deductively valid and each premise of each derivation belongs to K.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This filters systematizations: only derivations with deductive validity and premises from the base set K (later generalized to K*) are considered acceptable systematizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generating set for a set of derivations
rubrics_metrics.description: A generating set for a set of derivations Φ is a set of argument patterns Π such that each derivation in Φ instantiates some pattern in Π.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument patterns are built from schematic sentences plus filling instructions and a classification specifying roles; the generating set abstracts the recurring derivation patterns that produce Φ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Completeness of a generating set (w.r.t. K)
rubrics_metrics.description: A generating set Π for Φ is complete with respect to K iff every derivation which is acceptable relative to K and which instantiates a pattern in Π belongs to Φ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Completeness ensures the generating set actually accounts for all acceptable derivations of the systematization under consideration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Basis selection via paucity of patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: For each acceptable systematization, select a basis (a generating set complete w.r.t. K) which ranks best according to the criterion of paucity of patterns: fewer patterns is better.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paucity is the criterion used in step (3) of determining E(K); the quality of a generating set is inversely proportional to the number of patterns it contains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree of unification (unifying power) — size of conclusions vs number of patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: The degree of unification of a systematization Φ is directly proportional to the size of C(Φ) (the set of sentences occurring as conclusions of arguments in Φ) and inversely proportional to the number of patterns in the basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If numeric values could be given, one would rank systematizations by maximizing |C(Φ)| while minimizing number_of_patterns; this produces E(K) as the best systematization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stringency of patterns (mentioned but underdeveloped)
rubrics_metrics.description: Kitcher mentions a criterion of stringency of patterns as part of his list but does not provide a worked-out account of how stringency should affect unifying power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors note this criterion is left out of their exposition because Kitcher doesn't sufficiently develop it; it remains an open/unclear element in applying the model.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local vs global characterization of explanatoriness
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a particular argument counts as an explanation is not (for Kitcher) a purely local matter about that argument alone, but a global property tied to whether it belongs to the best systematization of beliefs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This rejects views that treat explanatoriness as an intrinsic, argument-level property; assessment depends on the comparative unifying role of the derivation within E(K).

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal notion of an argument pattern (schematic components)
rubrics_metrics.description: An argument pattern is given by a triple ⟨s,f,c⟩ where s is a schematic argument (sequence of schematic sentences), f is a set of sets of filling instructions (how to replace dummy letters), and c is a classification specifying roles of sentences in s.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text illustrates with a mathematical example (tangent line derivation) showing schematic sentences, filling instructions, and classification (which sentences are premises and which follow).

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow systematizations to appeal to a superset K* (K*-modification)
rubrics_metrics.description: A systematization of K may be any set of arguments which derive sentences in K from premises in K*, where K* is a consistent superset of K (possibly identical) that can be rationally accepted by those who accept K.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This modification is recommended to handle cases where explanatory improvements require richer language or new concepts (e.g., Lagrange, Galois), allowing cross-language/system comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniformity as a kind of unification / explanatory virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: A desirable feature of a systematization is that its argument patterns apply uniformly across cases (e.g., uniformly for all real closed fields), which counts as a form of unification and explanatory virtue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Brumfiel values proofs/methods that apply uniformly to all real closed fields; Kitcher’s machinery can capture uniformity as part of unifying power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical feasibility and illuminative/explanatory value (methodological virtue)
rubrics_metrics.description: Explanatory worth is not just a formal counting-of-patterns: methods that are theoretically unifying (e.g., Tarski–Seidenberg decision procedure) may fail to be explanatory in practice because they are infeasible, unwieldy, or do not illuminate why the result holds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors argue mathematical practice values proofs that provide insight and are usable; a systematization that is formally best but practically unusable may not be considered explanatorily privileged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systematization by conceptualization vs axiomatization
rubrics_metrics.description: Systematization by conceptualization consists in modifying the language so formerly disparate questions and solutions are brought under a common formulation, enabling perception of a common thread and increasing insight (e.g., Viète, Lagrange).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This counts as an explanatory improvement: adopting new concepts/language can reduce apparent dissimilarities and provide understanding beyond mere syntactic unification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanatory store E(K) as idealized best systematization
rubrics_metrics.description: E(K) is the explanatory store over K: the (idealized, unique) best systematization of K — i.e., the set of derivations that best balances paucity of patterns and breadth of conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kitcher idealizes E(K) as unique; authors critique that this idealization may conflict with mathematical practice and with cross-language/system comparisons unless modified with K*.
